headline: AI companies destroying books for data, investigation reveals
summary: A secret tracking device placed in a rare book led to an Amazon warehouse where employees reportedly cut spines off books to scan them for AI training.
details: An investigation by 404 Media has uncovered a disturbing practice where AI companies are allegedly acquiring millions of books, including rare editions, to train their models. In many cases, the books are destroyed in the process.

The investigation involved placing a tracking device in a rare book, which was then sent to an Amazon warehouse (VGT3) in Las Vegas. Employees at this facility reportedly spend their time cutting the spines off books and feeding them into scanners.

Sources within the facility claim its sole purpose is to scan books, with one employee stating, "All we do is scan books." A logo at VGT3 depicts a dinosaur appearing to rip apart a book, further suggesting the facility's destructive intent.

These large book orders have reportedly become more common in the AI era, with many suspecting they are not for readership but for training AI models. Booksellers note that rare books without ISBNs are typically excluded from these bulk orders.

This practice echoes previous revelations, such as Anthropic's 'Project Panama,' an initiative aimed at "destructively scan[ning] all the books in the world." While a judge permitted Anthropic to use books for AI training, the company faced a fine for possessing millions of pirated books.

Meta has also been implicated, with court filings revealing the company pirated nearly 82 terabytes of books. The demand for data by frontier AI models appears to be driving these aggressive acquisition and digitization efforts.

The cost-effectiveness of acquiring secondhand books in bulk from marketplaces like Biblio, rather than purchasing new digital versions, is likely a primary driver for these operations. This method allows AI companies to access vast amounts of text data for model training.
